title: Locally separated algebraic spaces are decent
statement: Let $X$ be an algebraic space over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ [def-trf-algebraic-space, def-weil-affine-spectrum], with point set and atlas topology [def-a1-space-point-topology] and sheaf fibre products [lem-trf-space-fibre-products-etale-covers]. An immersion of algebraic spaces means a representable morphism all of whose scheme base changes are immersions [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Call an algebraic space $X$ decent if every morphism $\operatorname{Spec}L\to X$ from a field spectrum is quasi-compact: for every affine scheme $U\to X$, the scheme $U\times_X\operatorname{Spec}L$ is quasi-compact [def-weil-pbc-quasi-compact-scheme]. If the absolute diagonal $X\to X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z}X$ is an immersion, then $X$ is decent. No quasi-separatedness or finite-type hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tag 088J (lemma-locally-separated-decent); decency is Tag 03I8 (definition-very-reasonable), equivalently condition (6) of Tag 03JV (lemma-UR-finite-above-x).

proof.text: Fix $x\in|X|$. Choose an etale scheme chart $V\to X$ and $v\in V$ over $x$, using the affine etale atlas. Write $u=\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(v)$ with its canonical map to $V$. This map is a monomorphism: two maps into $u$ with the same composite into $V$ agree on points, and their maps on local rings agree because the map $\mathcal O_{V,v}\to\kappa(v)$ is surjective; equality can be tested on these stalk maps. Form $H=u\times_Xu$. The map $H\to u\times_{\mathbf Z}u$ is the base change of the absolute diagonal of $X$, hence an immersion by hypothesis. The two kernel-relation projections, diagonal, interchange and composition make $(u,H)$ a groupoid: on test schemes its arrows are pairs with equal images in $X$. The map to the pair groupoid $(u,u\times_{\mathbf Z}u)$ preserves these operations. The field-groupoid lemma therefore makes this immersion a closed immersion.

The projection $u\times_XV\to u$ is etale by base change of the chart. It is a disjoint union of finite separable field spectra by the etale-fibre lemma. The map $H\to u\times_XV$ is a monomorphism, being the base change of $u\to V$. The field-coproduct monomorphism lemma says $H$ is a union of these components. It is also affine, since step 1 embeds it as a closed subscheme of the affine $u\times_{\mathbf Z}u$. Hence it is quasi-compact; its disjoint open components admit a finite subcover, so there are only finitely many of them. Thus $H$ is a finite union of open components of the etale $u$-scheme $u\times_XV$; an open immersion is etale and etale maps compose, so the first projection $H\to u$ is etale, and it is quasi-compact as $H$ is affine and $u$ has one point. Interchange switches the projections, so both are etale and quasi-compact. The finite-self-relation lemma supplies a field monomorphism $j:\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$.

Fix any affine etale chart $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\to X$ and put $F=U\times_X\operatorname{Spec}k$. It is etale over $k$, so write $F=\coprod_{i\in I}\operatorname{Spec}k_i$ with $k_i/k$ finite separable. The projection $F\to U$ is a monomorphism. For each component its map to $U$ factors through the residue field of its image point $p_i$; base changing this monomorphism by $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(p_i)\to U$ and applying the field-coproduct lemma shows $k_i=\kappa(p_i)$. The same lemma shows the $p_i$ are pairwise distinct: over a fixed $p$, that base change is a monomorphism to one field spectrum and has at most one component.

Set $R=U\times_XU$, and let $q:R\to P=U\times_{\mathbf Z}U$ be its immersion, again a pullback of the absolute diagonal. Factor it as a closed immersion $q^{\prime}:R\to P^{\prime}$ followed by an open immersion $P^{\prime}\subseteq P$. Write $e:U\to R$ for the relation diagonal. Both $R\to U$ and $\mathrm{id}_U$ are etale, so etale cancellation makes $e$ etale. It is a monomorphism, so the etale-monomorphism lemma makes it an open immersion. Also $q e=\Delta_U$ is a closed immersion: under the affine product identification it is induced by the surjection $A\otimes_{\mathbf Z}A\to A$, $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$. Since $q$ is an embedding, $e(U)=q^{-1}(\Delta_U(U))$ is closed in $R$. Thus $R=e(U)\amalg W$ for an open and closed complement $W$.

The subset $q^{\prime}(W)$ is closed in $P^{\prime}$, since $W$ is closed in $R$ and $q^{\prime}$ is a closed embedding. It is disjoint from $\Delta_U(U)$, which is contained in $P^{\prime}$. For an open subspace $P^{\prime}$, closure in $P$ restricted to $P^{\prime}$ is closure in $P^{\prime}$. Therefore $\overline{q(W)}\cap\Delta_U(U)=\varnothing$. This is solely the definition of closure, since every point of $P^{\prime}\setminus q^{\prime}(W)$ has an open neighbourhood there avoiding $q(W)$.

For $i\ne i^{\prime}$ the map $\operatorname{Spec}(k_i\otimes_k k_{i^{\prime}})\to R$ comes from $F\times_kF=U\times_X\operatorname{Spec}k\times_XU$, or directly from equality of the two composites to $X$. It avoids $e(U)$: the two projections land at distinct points $p_i,p_{i^{\prime}}$ of $U$, whereas both projections agree on $e(U)$. It therefore factors through the open complement $W$. If $I$ were infinite, choose countably many indices and apply the infinite-primes lemma to their distinct primes $p_i$ and the embeddings $k\hookrightarrow k_i=\kappa(p_i)$. It says the closure of the union of these cross-product images in $P=\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_{\mathbf Z}A)$ meets $\Delta_U(U)$. That union lies in $q(W)$, contradicting step 5. Thus $I$ is finite. A finite disjoint union of finite field extensions is finite over $k$: its coordinate algebra is a finite product of finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces.

We have proved finiteness of $U\times_X\operatorname{Spec}k$ for every affine etale chart $U\to X$. Apply the finite-chart decency criterion to the monomorphism $j$ from step 2. It gives quasi-compactness of every field-valued representative of $x$, on all affine scheme tests (not merely etale tests). As $x$ was arbitrary, every morphism $\operatorname{Spec}L\to X$ is quasi-compact. This is precisely the definition of decency in the statement. If $X$ is empty there are no such representatives and the assertion is vacuous.
